spec.title: Seats: names, caps, bring-up and down, status, the shared seat

item.title: A wake to a seat that is not there
Rows and codes this domain owns

spec.purpose: The seats domain knows every seat by name, sees whether it is absent, idle or busy, holds a bring-up that would pass a cap, and runs bring-up and down through the seat script on the host. It never starts an agent itself.

section.title: What the seats domain decides

node.title: A bring-up past its role's cap, or a down of a busy shared seat, is held and run when the way is clear; a seat script refusal is retried while its cause can clear and dead-lettered only after the last attempt

section.text: In: role files, the executor's observation verbs, the jobs that name a seat. Out: seat names, Seat statuses every tick, and the hold or release of seat jobs.

section.title: Seat names from role labels
section.text: The seat for a role on a ticket is the role file's label with the ticket variable replaced by the ticket id lowercased, the whole lowercased. A label that still holds a variable afterwards is an error naming the role.
A role whose label holds no ticket variable is a fixed seat shared by every ticket: the merger, the monitor, the orchestrator, the interface agent.
The reverse lookup, role of a seat name, tries every role file's label against the name with the ticket substituted; policies use it to wake the seat that asked.
Both are pure functions of the role files' labels, loaded once and reloaded with the configuration.

section.title: Observing seats: absent, idle, busy
section.text: Once per tick the observer runs the agent list verb: every agent herdr knows, with its name, status and pane. A seat with no agent of its name is absent.

Busy: herdr reports it busy, or the last lines of its pane match the configured busy pattern (a spinner), because herdr says idle while a seat runs a long command. The pane is read only for seats a verdict waits on.
A seat is idle when it is present, not busy, and its pane's last lines match the done pattern or show a prompt; Seat.Since is the first tick that saw the current status and resets on change.
When the agent list verb fails the status of every seat is unknown for that tick; nothing is judged on unknown, and the executor health domain says why.
Cost: the footer text of the agent runtime is the busy signal, so a change to that footer silences it; the patterns are configuration, not Go, so a change is one key.

section.title: Caps: hold, never refuse
section.text: Before a seat-up job runs, the live seats of its role are counted from the observation; when the count is at the role's cap the job is held with reason cap and looked at again every tick.
The seat script refuses over cap with exit 3 and a 429 record; holding before the call spares the refusal, the record and the retry, and keeps the order in which tickets asked.
A job held for cap longer than the configured cap wait raises one 500 note to the monitor naming the role and the ticket, latched per job, so a cap that never clears is seen.
Held seat-up jobs of one role release in the order of their record ids, oldest first.

section.title: Bring-up through the seat script
section.text: Bring-up is the seat-up verb: the seat script with the ticket and the role. It leases a slot, checks out the branch, builds the panes, starts the agent, binds the guard and sends the brief; the scheduler sees only the exit code.
A live seat is left as it is by the script, so the job runs for every record that says seat and never asks first; two bring-ups of one seat cost one call.

Exit 0: done. Exit 3: a refusal whose cause can clear (bring-up gate, slot not back, branch held elsewhere, foreign process in the slot), retried with backoff. Exit 4 or a timeout: retried. Exit 2: a bug, dead at once.

The branch case: a slot cannot be put on a branch another worktree holds, which clears when that worktree detaches; the retry carries it without reading the reason, and the last reason is in the dead-letter note if it never clears.
The prompt job that follows the bring-up waits for it to be done and is then confirmed like any wake.

section.title: Down, and the shared seat
section.text: Down is the seat-down verb with the seat name: the script retires the agent, closes the tab, returns the slot and records seat.down. A second down prints already down and exits 0.

Exit 3, a foreign process still in the slot, is retried with backoff because the process may leave; exit 4, a slot that would not come back, likewise; after the last attempt the dead-letter note names the seat and the last reason.

A down of a shared seat is held while that seat is busy or while a prompt job to it is still confirming, and runs when it is idle: a merged record for one ticket must not end the merger another ticket's review just woke.
Cost: a shared seat that idles between two tickets is downed and seated again; the alternative, one merger per ticket, is a role label change the architect owns.

section.title: A wake to a seat that is not there
section.text: A prompt job whose seat is absent is held with reason absent and re-examined every tick; the row said wake, not seat, so the scheduler never seats it. After the configured absent wait the job is dead with a 500 note naming the seat.
The supervisor re-seats fixed seats that died; a hold gives it the time, where the bash runner wrote a 500 at once and lost the wake.

section.title: Leases: who holds what
section.text: The slot lease belongs to the seat script and the pool; the scheduler never leases or returns a slot.
The ticket lease belongs to the queue; the scheduler enqueues through the queue verb and sweeps expired leases through the sweep verb on the health domain's schedule.
The seat lease is the agent answering and the seat record carrying no end; the observer is its proof, and an absent seat with a job waiting is the stall the health domain reports.

section.title: Rows and codes this domain owns
section.owns-code: The seat script's refusal when a role is at its cap. The scheduler holds before the call and never writes a 429 itself; one it reads is a note for the board.
